title: Bleed the air out of a brake caliper, shutting the bleeder each cycle before the pedal comes back up
instruction: Bleed the air out of this brake caliper.
context: Automotive service technicians and mechanics (O*NET 49-3023.00; about 826,000 US jobs, BLS) bleed brakes as a regular part of brake work, after a caliper or line is replaced: air in the line compresses, so the pedal is spongy and the car takes longer to stop. In the two-person pedal method one hand presses the pedal and keeps it down, the other opens the caliper's bleeder about a quarter turn so fluid and air push out into a catch jar and the pedal sinks, shuts it while the pedal is still down, and only then does the pedal come up; this repeats until no bubbles come out. Shop bleeding guides give this order because the master cylinder's piston springs back on the pedal's return and pulls on the line, so a bleeder that is still open draws air back in. Unlike tasks that hold a pedal while the other hand works, the score is the air left after repeated cycles, and each wrong release puts air back.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A bench brake trainer, fixed to the table except for the pedal and the wrench. Pedal stand: a steel post 3 x 4 cm on a 12 x 10 cm foot plate, with the pedal's hinge at x 38, y 16, 8 cm up; a steel pedal lever 11 cm long runs from the hinge toward the robot to a black rubber pad 4.5 x 5 x 1.2 cm centered at x 27, y 16, its top 9 cm up at rest. The pedal goes down 3.3 cm at the pad (17 degrees) to a floor stop and a return spring brings it back up (about 2 N at rest, 4.5 N fully down). Behind the hinge, an aluminum master cylinder (3.2 cm across, 7 cm long, along x) with a translucent reservoir (6 x 4 x 4.5 cm, MIN and MAX lines, amber fluid) on top. The pedal's pushrod works its piston (19 mm bore) through a short arm, which covers the compensating port in the first 8% of the stroke and then pushes 4.2 mL into the line by the floor stop. With the bleeder shut, a push of about 6 N on the pad (6 psi in the line, a light push for one arm) stops the pedal partway down on the fluid, about 16% of its stroke with the starting air and about 9% once bled; with the bleeder open, the pedal sinks to the floor as fluid leaves. A car's pedal makes hundreds of psi; 6 psi is scaled to what the YAM can push, since the scored skill is the hydraulic order of events (press, open, shut, release), not the pressure. A 4.8 mm steel brake line runs from it along the table to a black cast-iron disc-brake caliper (9 x 6 x 6 cm) on a steel bracket, centered at x 30, y -12, from 3 to 9 cm up. The bleeder screw stands on the caliper's top at x 29, y -11 (an 11 mm hex, 12.7 mm across its corners, with a yellow paint ring and a nipple up to 11.8 cm). An 11 mm chrome box-end wrench is on the bleeder's hex: its handle is 12.5 cm long from the bleeder's axis, 1.6 cm wide and 0.8 cm thick, 10 cm up, and points along -y (bleeder shut) at the start; turned a quarter turn counterclockwise seen from above it points along +x (bleeder open), with click detents at shut and open and stops 3 degrees past each. A clear vinyl hose (4.8 mm inside, 8 mm outside) runs from the nipple up and over to a glass catch jar (7 cm across, 9 cm tall, in a wire holder) at x 21.5, y -4.5 holding 4.5 cm of dark old fluid, its end held 2 cm under the fluid inside an inverted graduated tube (1 cm across) that collects the air. The caliper and its line hold 8 mL, with 1.2 mL of air in them at the start; the bleeder is shut and the pedal is up. The real rig uses a clear-body caliper of the same size, so the air in it can be seen.
scoring: The score reads the air left in the caliper, because that air is what makes the pedal spongy and the car slow to stop. Air drawn back in, latched: 0 if more than 0.01 mL of air (one bubble, about 3 mm across) enters the caliper at any time. Air enters when the pedal comes up with the bleeder still open past 20 degrees, where it starts passing fluid: the master cylinder's piston, coming back on its spring, pulls about 5 psi of suction on the line, and air comes in around the bleeder's threads, which do not seal once its seat lifts. With the bleeder shut first, the piston only takes back what it pushed and no air enters. It stays latched because the order is the procedure's one rule, and the air let in would take more cycles to push out again. In a real trial, check on the video that the wrench was back inside a witness mark 20 degrees from shut before the pedal started up, and watch the real rig's clear-body caliper and the clear bleeder hose, where air drawn in shows as bubbles rising. At the end, also 0 if a gripper still touches the pedal pad or the wrench (its palm or fingers within 2 mm, the solver's resting gap: a hand still on either can hold the pedal down or turn the bleeder, so the job is not finished; video); if the pedal or the wrench still moves faster than 0.2 rad/s (still settling; video); if the wrench is more than 10 degrees from shut, outside its shut detent (the bleeder left open can leak fluid onto the caliper; witness mark); or if the pedal is more than 8% of its stroke (2.6 mm at the pad) down or its piston not back, since that keeps the compensating port shut and seals the line off from the reservoir, so the brake can drag (ruler at the pad). Otherwise by the air left in a final state held 1 s, read in a real trial as 1.2 mL minus the jar's graduated tube: 1.0 at 0.2 mL or less, the firm pedal a technician checks for (four correct cycles leave 0.15 mL, three leave 0.25 mL); 0.5 at 0.36 mL or less, 70% out but the pedal still a little soft, so the car is not ready (three cycles; two leave 0.42 mL); 0.25 at 0.84 mL or less, at least 30% out, real progress but still spongy (one cycle leaves 0.72 mL); 0 above that. Doing nothing, pumping the pedal with the bleeder shut, or opening the bleeder without pressing leave all 1.2 mL in and score 0. Where the arms end up does not count. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0. The volumes are scaled (1.2 mL of air in an 8 mL line) so that a few cycles clear it.
reset_notes: Put the wrench back at shut (pointing -y) and the pedal up. In the real rig, inject 1.2 mL of air into the caliper by syringe through its fill port, refill and re-invert the graduated tube in the jar, and top the reservoir up to MAX.
fidelity: No fluid is simulated: a pressure model of the line, caliper, jar and reservoir tracks the air in the caliper, shown as a white disc on its top whose area follows it, with bubbles at the jar as air leaves. The pedal moves with that model: pressed, it stops where the line reaches 6 psi and sinks only as fluid leaves the open bleeder; let up, its piston draws on the line. A real trial reads the air from the jar's graduated tube and the pedal's travel from a ruler.
